name: Cost of Tree
description: For a tree $$$T$$$ with root $$$r$$$, where each node $$$u$$$ has a value $$$a_u$$$ associated with it, the cost of the tree defined as: $$$$$$\sum_{u\in T} (a_u \cdot d(r,u))$$$$$$ Here, this sum is taken over all nodes $$$u$$$ in the tree $$$T$$$, and $$$d(r,u)$$$ denotes the number of edges on the shortest path from node $$$r$$$ to node $$$u$$$ on a tree. You are given a tree consisting of $$$n$$$ nodes, rooted at node $$$1$$$. Each node $$$i$$$ has a value $$$a_i$$$ assigned to it. For each $$$r$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, please solve the following problem independently: Consider the subtree of node $$$r$$$ with respect to node $$$1$$$. Formally, the subtree of node $$$r$$$ is the tree consisting of all nodes $$$u$$$ such that the shortest path from $$$1$$$ to $$$u$$$ contains $$$r$$$. Find the maximum cost of the subtree after performing at most one operation of the following type on the subtree: Choose any node $$$u$$$ ($$$u \neq r$$$). Remove the edge from $$$u$$$ to the parent of node $$$u$$$$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$. Then, add an edge from $$$u$$$ to any node $$$v$$$ that is still reachable from $$$r$$$. It can be shown that after this operation, the graph remains a tree. As an example, below shows an example of an operation with $$$r=1$$$,$$$u=5$$$, and $$$v=4$$$. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$Formally, remove the edge from $$$u$$$ to $$$p$$$, where $$$p$$$ is the unique node satisfying $$$d(u,p)=1$$$ and $$$d(u,r)=d(p,r)+1$$$
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each testcase contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the count of nodes in the tree. The second line of each testcase contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$). Then $$$n − 1$$$ lines follow, the $$$i$$$-th line containing two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$) — the two nodes that the $$$i$$$-th edge connects. It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$ over all test cases.
output_specification: For each test case, print $$$n$$$ numbers – the answers for $$$r=1,2,\ldots,n$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2192D — Cost of Tree [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
